study_identification.title: Normative Modeling of Brain Morphometry in Clinical High Risk for Psychosis

study_characteristics.study_objective: To quantify deviations from the normative range of neuroanatomical variation in individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR-P) and evaluate their overlap with healthy variation and their association with positive symptoms, cognition, and conversion to a psychotic disorder.

dataset_name.answer: Independent multisite sample for normative modeling (37,407 healthy individuals from 81 datasets); see Ge et al. 2023 for details

hc_age.answer: aged 3-90 years; mean age not specified; see Ge et al. 2023

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer (versions 5.1 to 7.0 across sites); ENIGMA quality assessment pipeline

quality_checking_detail.answer: Standardized ENIGMA quality assessment procedures for FreeSurfer output; extreme values in each site-dataset identified and removed using the interquartile range (IQR) method during data preparation

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: ComBat-GAM (Combatting Batch Effects - Generalized Additive Model) used for site harmonization in the normative model training; optimal covariate combination involved site harmonization (ComBat-GAM) and the inclusion of intracranial volume, mean CT, and mean SA in the models of the regional measures of SV, CT, and SA, respectively

model_origin_detail.answer: CentileBrain reference normative models trained on 37,407 healthy individuals (53.3% female; aged 3-90 years) from 81 datasets using Multivariable Fractional Polynomial Regression (MFPR). Models developed by ENIGMA Lifespan Group. See Ge et al., 2023 (BioRxiv, doi:10.1101/2023.01.30.523509) for details. Models publicly available at https://centilebrain.org/

response_variable.answer: Cortical thickness (68 regions); Cortical surface area (68 regions); Subcortical volume (14 regions)

predictor_variables.answer: Age; Sex; Site/Scanner; ICV (for SV models); Mean CT (for CT models); Mean SA (for SA models)

predictor_effects.answer: Age: fixed effect modeled with fractional polynomials; Sex: sex-specific models (stratified); Site: handled via ComBat-GAM harmonization; ICV/Mean CT/Mean SA: fixed effects as covariates

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly addresses multiple aspects of nuisance structure. Site effects are handled via ComBat-GAM harmonization. Scanner/acquisition differences are addressed through the harmonization procedure. Global measures (ICV, mean CT, mean SA) are included as covariates to account for variance differences. The normative modeling framework (CentileBrain) was optimized through benchmarking of 8 different algorithms and evaluation of 10 covariates pertaining to site, acquisition features, parcellation software version, and global neuroimaging measures. The model uses fractional polynomial regression which can capture nonlinear age effects. Quality control removes extreme values using IQR method.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Through this pipeline, we identified multivariable fractional polynomial regression as the optimal algorithm; the optimal covariate combination involved site harmonization (ComBat-GAM [combatting batch effects-generalized additive model]) and the inclusion of intracranial volume, mean CT, and mean SA in the models of the regional measures of SV, CT, and SA, respectively. ... Data preparation: Sex-specific subsamples of each pooled sample were randomly split into a training subset (80%) and a test subset (20%) stratified by scanning site. In each subset, data were mean-centered after extreme values in each site-dataset were identified and removed using the interquartile range (IQR) method; (ii) site harmonization was implemented using ComBat-GAM

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The normative model was trained using 5-fold cross-validation (5F-CV) in the sex-specific training subset (80% of data), which provides within-training-dataset validation using non-independent resampling approach.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Initially, models were trained using 5-fold crossvalidation (5F-CV) in the corresponding sex-specific training subset with age being the only explanatory variable and then model parameters were tested in the corresponding sex-specific test subset. Model performance was evaluated using the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The data were randomly split into training (80%) and test (20%) subsets stratified by scanning site. Model parameters trained in the training subset were then tested in the independent test subset from the same domain (healthy individuals, same 81 datasets). Performance metrics (MAE, RMSE) were evaluated on this held-out test set.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Sex-specific subsamples of each pooled sample were randomly split into a training subset (80%) and a test subset (20%) stratified by scanning site. ... Initially, models were trained using 5-fold crossvalidation (5F-CV) in the corresponding sex-specific training subset with age being the only explanatory variable and then model parameters were tested in the corresponding sex-specific test subset. Model performance was evaluated using the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The normative models were trained on an independent reference sample (37,407 healthy individuals from 81 datasets via CentileBrain) and then applied to a completely different domain dataset: the ENIGMA CHR-P Working Group sample (1,340 CHR-P individuals and 1,237 healthy controls from 29 international sites). The application to this external clinical dataset represents validation in a different domain. Furthermore, the paper reports sensitivity analyses using alternate normative models (Gaussian Process Regression, GAMLSS), alternate spatial resolutions (Schaefer 400 parcellation, gray and white matter maps), and reports that results were robust across these variations.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: the normative models for each regional measure in the framework were developed using data from an independent multisite sample of 37,407 healthy individuals (53.3% female; aged 3-90 years) (eMethods in Supplement 1). ... This case-control study used clinical-, IQ-, and neuroimaging software (FreeSurfer)-derived regional measures of cortical thickness (CT), cortical surface area (SA), and subcortical volume (SV) from 1340 individuals with CHR-P and 1237 healthy individuals pooled from 29 international sites participating in the Enhancing Neuroimaging Genetics Through Meta-analysis (ENIGMA) Clinical High Risk for Psychosis Working Group. ... We tested the robustness of the results to the spatial resolution of the input data and algorithm by repeating the normative analyses using the Schaeffer 400-parcels atlas or gray and white matter maps as input features and gaussian process regression or generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape as alternate algorithms

clinical_groups_n.answer: CHR-P:1340; CHR-P converted (CHR-PC):157; CHR-P not converted (CHR-PNC):940

clinical_groups_age.answer: All CHR-P: mean 20.75 (SD 4.74); CHR-PC: mean 20.09 (SD 4.68); CHR-PNC: mean and SD not separately reported

clinical_groups_sex.answer: All CHR-P: F 47.09% M 52.91%; CHR-PC: F 40.76% M 59.24%; CHR-PNC: sex distribution not separately reported

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score computed by subtracting the estimated normative value from the raw value and dividing by the root mean square error of the model; infranormal defined as z < -1.96 (5th percentile); supranormal defined as z > 1.96 (95th percentile); Average Deviation Score (ADS) computed by averaging regional z-scores for CT, SA, SV, and globally

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Two-proportion z tests to compare proportion of individuals with infra- or supranormal z-scores between groups; Linear support vector classification with 10-fold cross-validation to estimate diagnostic status using regional z-scores; Linear regression models to assess associations between z-scores/ADS and positive symptoms and IQ (with and without site as random effect); Brain Basis Set (BBS) multivariate estimation modeling to identify multivariate patterns of associations; Leave-one-site-out analysis for robustness; Analyses repeated separately for CHR-PC and CHR-PNC subgroups; FDR correction for multiple comparisons (P < 0.05)
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Regional variation in brain morphometry of CHR-P individuals was largely nested within healthy variation and had negligible value for diagnosis, cognition, positive symptoms, and conversion status.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Individuals with CHR-P and healthy individuals showed complete overlap in distributions of z-scores and observed values. For any given region, the proportion with infranormal or supranormal values was low (<11.42%) and similar between CHR-P and healthy individuals. Linear support vector classifiers using z-scores or observed measures could not distinguish CHR-P from healthy individuals (AUC 0.53 and 0.56) or CHR-PC from healthy individuals (AUC 0.52 and 0.47). However, a significantly higher percentage of CHR-P had infranormal global ADS (4.18% vs 1.70%, P=6.85×10^-4), SV ADS (4.03% vs 1.94%, P=0.02), and SA ADS (3.43% vs 1.05%, P=2.53×10^-4) compared to healthy individuals. Within CHR-P, only SA ADS showed weak associations with positive symptoms (β=-0.08, 95%CI -0.13 to -0.02, P=0.02) and IQ (β=0.09, 95%CI 0.02-0.15, P=0.02), though the positive symptom association did not persist when including site as random effect. A higher percentage of CHR-PC (5.10%) than healthy individuals (0.89%) had infranormal z-scores for right inferior temporal thickness (P=0.01), and a higher percentage of CHR-PC (7.01%) than CHR-PNC (1.38%) had infranormal z-scores for right superior temporal sulcus surface area (P=4.69×10^-3). Traditional case-control comparisons replicated previous findings of very small effect size (<0.22) cortical thickness decrements in CHR-P.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Cross-sectional data do not capture potential longitudinal changes that may be more informative. Multi-site data collection with different scanners and protocols may introduce residual site effects despite harmonization and leave-one-site-out robustness analyses. The study focuses on macroscale morphometric measures and does not examine microstructural or functional measures that might provide additional information.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Authors suggest macroscale neuromorphometric measures have limited utility as diagnostic biomarkers of psychosis risk. The findings support the notion that brain morphological changes in CHR-P states are minimal, with variation nested within normal range for the majority of individuals. Only a small minority of CHR-PC showed pronounced decrements in temporal regions. The study demonstrates the value of normative modeling approaches in characterizing individual-level deviations while revealing substantial overlap with healthy variation.

general_notes.general_notes: This is the largest neuroimaging dataset of CHR-P individuals to date, utilizing the ENIGMA CHR-P Working Group sample (29 sites). The normative models were based on the CentileBrain framework developed by the ENIGMA Lifespan Group, which benchmarked 8 different algorithms and optimized covariates. The study used pre-trained normative models from an independent large reference sample (37,407 individuals from 81 datasets). FreeSurfer versions ranged from 5.1 to 7.0 across sites. The study included extensive supplementary and sensitivity analyses: alternate ADS definitions, alternate normative models (GPR, GAMLSS), alternate spatial resolutions (Schaefer 400 parcellation, voxel-based gray/white matter), CHR-P subsyndrome analyses (APS, BIPS, GRD), leave-one-site-out analyses, and medication status analyses. Follow-up data available for 1,097 CHR-P individuals (mean 19.71 months, SD 13.97). CHR-P status assessed using SIPS (806 participants) or CAARMS (534 participants). The study represents a comprehensive application of normative modeling to characterize individual-level brain variation in psychosis risk states.
